Source. After HDLC strips delimiters and FCS, this read consumes the second Spinel frame's `28 00` length field and materializes `frameLen = 40` plus `framePtr` to the forwarded UDP payload beginning `16 02 20 20 ...`.

The trailing two bytes of the same Spinel frame are `bf f0`, so this read sets `sockPort = 61631` (`kCoapUdpPort`). That destination-port state is what routes the forwarded payload into the CoAP receive path.

With `messageInfo.mSockPort = 61631`, this call hands the attacker-controlled 40-byte blob to the UDP receiver. The saved ASan stack shows the same flow continuing into `Coap::CoapBase::ProcessReceivedRequest()`.

CoAP header parsing treats the 40-byte blob as a request: first byte `0x16` yields token length 6 and non-confirmable type bits, `code = 0x02` is POST, and option walking begins at payload byte 10. Five successive `0x20` headers contribute zero-length deltas that advance the option number to 10; `0x15` then yields URI-Path option 11 with length 5, value bytes `61 2f 61 71 00`, and the next byte `0xff` is the payload marker. `MoveOffset()` therefore advances the message offset to 22, leaving an 18-byte body beginning `00 ff 00 00...`.
`ProcessReceivedRequest()` copies the step-4 URI-Path option value into `uriPath`, so `uriPath == "a/aq"` and the request is dispatched into `AddressResolver::HandleAddressQuery()`.

`HandleAddressQuery()` asks `ThreadTlv::GetTlv(..., ThreadTlv::kTarget, sizeof(targetTlv), targetTlv)` for a target TLV. Starting from `aMessage.GetOffset() == 22`, `Tlv::GetOffset()` reads header bytes `00 ff`; because the length byte is `kExtendedLength`, it reads the next two bytes as `extLength = 0x0000` and accepts the current body offset as the `kTarget` TLV.

`Tlv::Get()` first preserves the parsed header byte `mLength = 0xff`, then `aMessage.Read(offset, aMaxLength, &aTlv)` copies only the fixed 18-byte `ThreadTargetTlv` object. The resulting stack object therefore carries attacker-controlled length `0xff` but materializes a 16-byte all-zero `targetTlv.GetTarget()`.

Root cause. `ThreadTargetTlv::IsValid()` only checks `GetLength() >= 16`, so the `0xff` header from step 7 passes. Vulnerable `HandleAddressQuery()` then proceeds without `targetTlv.Init()`, leaving that inbound TLV header live for later serialization; the fix inserts the missing reset immediately after this line.

This guard determines whether the unicast response path is taken. The source-grounded state from step 7 is the all-zero IPv6 address, and `Netif::IsUnicastAddress()` only scans the current unicast list for equality. The saved ASan stack nevertheless places the reproduced run at line 605, so this guard evaluated true at runtime, but the staged artifacts do not reveal which unicast-list state made it true.
Because step 9's guard passed on the reproduced run, line 605 passes the same stack `targetTlv` by reference into `SendAddressQueryResponse()` without any intervening `targetTlv.Init()`.

At `SendAddressQueryResponse()` line 647, the same object reaches `message->AppendTlv(aTargetTlv)`. `AppendTlv()` passes `aTlv.GetSize()` to `Append()`, so the outbound copy length is derived from the preserved TLV header length rather than the fixed `ThreadTargetTlv` C++ size.
